newsitem.title: USA: Oil up sharply; corn, wheat prices rise.
newsitem.headline: Oil up sharply; corn, wheat prices rise.

text.p: Heating oil prices rose sharply on Wednesday on concerns about supply after the American Petroleum Institute (API) said heating oil inventories are significanly below year-earlier levels.
Corn and wheat prices closed higher on signs of surprisingly strong commercial demand for grains despite upcoming harvest supplies.
Heating oil for October delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange settled up 2.28 cent to 67.87 cents a gallon after rising as high as 68.00 cents a gallon.
October crude oil closed up 58 cents to $23.89 a barrel, while October gasoline closed up 0.32 cent to 63.06 cents a gallon.
"The heating oil rally was spelled A-P-I," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group. "It's a very tight inventory situation."

On Tuesday evening, API said total distillate stocks, of which heating oil is a component, grew a mere 235,000 barrels for the week ended Sept. 13, when traders had been expecting a two million-barrel build to prepare for the winter.

"The high need for distillate in July, (whether through U.S. demand or exports), coupled with only modest production, is giving rise to growing concerns over distillate stock levels for the upcoming winter," Energy Information Administration chief Jay Hakes told a conference for U.S. energy officials Monday.
Heating oil stocks are 20.7 million barrels below a year ago, and most of the shortfall is in the northeastern United States, the largest market in the world for heating oil.

Heating oil is also in tight supply in Europe. Analysts said U.S. exports of heating oil have increased while imports have decreased, signalling a possible competition between Europe and United States for supply.
Gas oil, the equivalent of heating oil in Europe, for October delivery rose $4.00 to $218.50 a metric ton Wednesday on London's International Petroleum Exchange.

At the Chicago Board of Trade September wheat closed 9-1/2 cents a bushel higher at $4.32-1/2 and September corn closed up 4-1/4 cents at $3.55-1/2. September soybeans gained 4-1/2 cents at $8.19-1/2.
Traders said the strong gains indicated greater than expected near-term demand by processors and exporters.
Harvest supplies from southern U.S. states have already begun trickling into the supply pipeline. But the main corn harvest from Ohio to Nebraska doesn't usually get in full swing until Oct. 1.
Corn and soybean growth is also behind schedule this year due to planting delays and cold weather.
"The trade still doesn't know the crop size on corn and beans. That's up to Mother Nature," said analyst Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.

Traders pointed to a cash delivery of 700,000 bushels of wheat posted on the September wheat contract on Wednesday that was received by Continental Grain, a major exporter and a bellwether for indicating cash market demand.

Sentiment also got a boost from statements by Guy LeGras, a senior European Union farm official, estimating a European grain harvest of 193 million to 194 million metric tons, a record but below the 200 million tons that the market has been expecting.

LeGras also said he did not see a grain export subsidy war with the United States restarting this year now that Europe looked to have a grain surplus. European subsidies have been suspended for more than a year to conserve supplies.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange pork belly futures closed strong on cash market demand, with February bellies up the 2 cent per pound trading limit at 78.55 cents.
During the day cash market traders reported that prices for cash bellies, the raw material for bacon manufacturers, rose to $70 per hundred pounds, the highest level since September 3.
Consumer demand may also be returning, traders said.
"We had a late tomato crop," said Bill Cipolla, belly trader for Iowa Grain, which he said could point to a pickup in bacon demand for bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwiches.
November lumber futures closed strong on cash demand at $351.50 per thousand board feet, up $8.40.

Cash market prices are well above futures and a seasonal setback in cash prices has been expected. Cash lumber prices will likely post a sharp fall in the next few weeks and narrow the gap they have with futures, traders said.
